hints: Look at Fig. 6.1 - generation 0 is the single trachea, and generation 1 is the first time it splits into two tubes going to each lung.
walkthrough:
Trace the branching in Fig. 6.1**
The trachea is generation 0, a single tube. It divides into two. Those two tubes each enter one lung, so you can picture air going left and right.

Name the first branches**
The two tubes that branch directly off the trachea are the left and right bronchi. After that they branch further into smaller bronchi and then bronchioles.
Final answer: bronchi (left and right bronchus)

hints: Think about what makes alveoli good for gas exchange - thin wall, close to capillaries, slow air movement - and check if generations 0 to 16 have those features.
Think about two problems: the physical barrier gases would have to cross in these large airways, and whether the blood around them has the right concentration gradient for exchange.
walkthrough:
Why distance matters**
Efficient gas exchange needs a very short diffusion distance - one thin squamous cell plus capillary endothelium. Generations 0 to 16 have thick walls with cartilage, smooth muscle, ciliated epithelium and mucus. That means many layers to cross, so diffusion would be far too slow.

Why time and blood supply matter**
Air flows fast through these conducting airways during ventilation, so there is little time for diffusion. Also, their blood comes from the systemic circulation via a branch of the aorta, not the pulmonary artery. That blood is already oxygenated, so there is no steep concentration gradient for oxygen to diffuse in or carbon dioxide to diffuse out.

Final answer: Diffusion distance too great / walls too thick with many cell layers and tissues to cross so diffusion too slow. Blood supply is systemic from aorta, already oxygenated, so no concentration gradient for O2/CO2.

hints: Focus only on the hatched Weibel bars in Fig. 6.2 and follow them from generation 0 on the left to generation 5 on the right.
walkthrough:
Read the Weibel trend**
Look at the hatched bars: generation 0 is about $1.8 \text{ cm}$, generation 1 about $1.2 \text{ cm}$, falling to about $0.35 \text{ cm}$ at generation 5. The bars get shorter to the right.

State the relationship**
That is an inverse correlation. Higher generation number means smaller lumen diameter, which fits branching into narrower airways.
Final answer: As airway generation number increases, airway diameter decreases.

hints: Start by comparing the heights of the white and grey MRI bars with the hatched Weibel bar in each generation group - do they follow the same falling pattern?
Pick out one or two actual values to quote, for example at generations 2, 3 or 4, to show how close the MRI results are to the standard.
Remember the stem information about HRCT and radiation - what practical advantage does MRI have for a patient who needs repeated checks of lung disease?
walkthrough:
Give a judgement with similarity**
Yes, HP gas MRI looks useful. Both projection and multi-Slice bars decrease from generation 0 to 5 just like the Weibel Lung model, and the values are close to the standard.

Support with data from Fig. 6.2**
For example, at generation 2 projection is about $0.93 \text{ cm}$, multi-Slice about $0.87 \text{ cm}$ and Weibel about $0.83 \text{ cm}$. At generation 3 all three are about $0.56$ to $0.62 \text{ cm}$. At generation 4 all three are about $0.40$ to $0.45 \text{ cm}$. That close agreement supports validity.

Add the safety advantage**
Unlike HRCT, HP gas MRI involves no harmful radiation exposure. That means it can be used repeatedly on the same person without risk, which is ideal for monitoring progression of pulmonary disease.

Final answer: Yes, useful. Both MRI methods show same trend of decreasing diameter with increasing generation and give similar values to Weibel, e.g. generation 2 about 0.93, 0.87, 0.83 cm and generation 3 about 0.62, 0.60, 0.56 cm for projection, multi-Slice and Weibel. No harmful radiation so can be repeated regularly to follow disease progression.
